fields.Question: Coding: given the raw bytes of an HTTP/1.1 request, parse the method, path, headers and body. What edge cases do you handle?
fields.Answer:
def parse_request(raw: bytes):
    head, sep, rest = raw.partition(b"\r\n\r\n")
    if not sep:
        raise ValueError("incomplete headers")
    lines = head.decode("iso-8859-1").split("\r\n")
    method, target, version = lines[0].split(" ")
    if not version.startswith("HTTP/1."):
        raise ValueError("unsupported version")
    headers = {}
    for line in lines[1:]:
        name, colon, value = line.partition(":")
        if not colon or not name or name != name.strip():
            raise ValueError("bad header line")
        key = name.lower()
        value = value.strip()
        headers[key] = f"{headers[key]}, {value}" if key in headers else value
    if "transfer-encoding" in headers:
        raise NotImplementedError("chunked body")
    length = int(headers.get("content-length", "0"))
    if len(rest) < length:
        raise ValueError("incomplete body")
    return method, target, headers, rest[:length]

Edge cases: header names are case insensitive; repeated headers combine with commas (except Set-Cookie); whitespace before the colon is invalid; both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length present is a request smuggling risk and must be rejected or handled per the RFC; limit header size and count; on a keep-alive connection the remaining bytes after the body belong to the next request.

Complexity: O(n) in request size.

Follow-ups: make it incremental for a streaming socket (a state machine), add chunked decoding, why proxies and servers disagreeing on parsing causes smuggling.
fields.Hint: Split head and body at CRLF CRLF; headers are case insensitive; body length comes from Content-Length.
fields.Fact: HTTP/1.1 framing is CRLF delimited headers plus Content-Length or chunked; ambiguity is a security bug.
fields.Source:
RFC 9112 HTTP/1.1 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112)
RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

fields.Question: Coding: decode a body sent with Transfer-Encoding: chunked.
fields.Answer:
def decode_chunked(data: bytes) -> bytes:
    body = bytearray()
    pos = 0
    while True:
        line_end = data.index(b"\r\n", pos)
        size = int(data[pos:line_end].split(b";")[0], 16)
        pos = line_end + 2
        if size == 0:
            return bytes(body)
        body += data[pos:pos + size]
        if data[pos + size:pos + size + 2] != b"\r\n":
            raise ValueError("missing CRLF after chunk")
        pos += size + 2

Format: each chunk is a hexadecimal size (optionally followed by ;extensions), CRLF, that many bytes, CRLF. A 0 size chunk ends the body, optionally followed by trailer fields and a final CRLF.

Why it exists: lets a server stream a response whose length it does not know in advance while keeping the connection reusable. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 do not use it; their framing replaces it.

Edge cases: chunk extensions, trailers, data split across socket reads (real decoders are incremental), absurd sizes (cap them).

Complexity: O(n).

Follow-ups: make it a generator over a socket, what happens when a proxy and a server disagree on Content-Length vs chunked.

fields.Question: Coding: implement a function that checks whether an IPv4 address belongs to a CIDR block like 10.1.0.0/16, without the ipaddress module. Then extend it to find the most specific matching route from a list.
fields.Answer:
def ip_to_int(ip: str) -> int:
    parts = ip.split(".")
    if len(parts) != 4:
        raise ValueError(ip)
    value = 0
    for part in parts:
        if not part.isdigit() or int(part) > 255 or (len(part) > 1 and part[0] == "0"):
            raise ValueError(ip)
        value = value << 8 | int(part)
    return value

def in_cidr(ip: str, cidr: str) -> bool:
    network, prefix = cidr.split("/")
    prefix = int(prefix)
    mask = (0xFFFFFFFF << (32 - prefix)) & 0xFFFFFFFF
    return ip_to_int(ip) & mask == ip_to_int(network) & mask

def best_route(ip: str, routes: dict[str, str]):
    matches = [(int(c.split("/")[1]), hop) for c, hop in routes.items() if in_cidr(ip, c)]
    return max(matches, default=(None, None))[1]

Complexity: in_cidr is O(1); best_route is O(R) per lookup. Real routers use a trie (binary or compressed) keyed by prefix bits for O(32) lookups.

Edge cases: /0 (mask 0, matches everything), /32, leading zeros (ambiguous octal in some parsers, reject them), network address with host bits set.

In practice: use ipaddress.ip_address(ip) in ipaddress.ip_network(cidr), which also handles IPv6.

Follow-ups: build the trie, check if two CIDR blocks overlap, split a block into subnets.

fields.Question: Coding: given a string, return 'IPv4', 'IPv6' or 'Neither' (LeetCode 468 style). Valid IPv4 is four decimal octets 0 to 255 without leading zeros; valid IPv6 here is eight groups of 1 to 4 hex digits.
fields.Answer:
HEX = set("0123456789abcdefABCDEF")

def valid_ip_address(s: str) -> str:
    if s.count(".") == 3:
        parts = s.split(".")
        if all(p.isdigit() and p.isascii() and len(p) <= 3 and int(p) <= 255
               and (p == "0" or p[0] != "0") for p in parts):
            return "IPv4"
    elif s.count(":") == 7:
        parts = s.split(":")
        if all(1 <= len(p) <= 4 and set(p) <= HEX for p in parts):
            return "IPv6"
    return "Neither"

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the split.

Edge cases: empty parts ('1..2.3', trailing dot), leading zeros ('01'), signs and spaces, non ASCII digits (str.isdigit accepts other scripts, hence isascii), more than 4 hex digits.

Real world caveat: real IPv6 allows :: compression and embedded IPv4; production code should use ipaddress, and say so in the interview.

Follow-ups: support :: compression, canonicalize an IPv6 address.

fields.Question: Coding: implement an in-process DNS cache for a resolver function that respects TTLs, caches failures briefly, and bounds memory.
fields.Answer:
import time
from collections import OrderedDict

class DnsCache:
    def __init__(self, resolve, max_entries=10_000, negative_ttl=5.0, clock=time.monotonic):
        self.resolve = resolve
        self.max_entries = max_entries
        self.negative_ttl = negative_ttl
        self.clock = clock
        self.entries = OrderedDict()

    def lookup(self, name):
        now = self.clock()
        entry = self.entries.get(name)
        if entry and entry[1] > now:
            self.entries.move_to_end(name)
            if isinstance(entry[0], Exception):
                raise entry[0]
            return entry[0]
        try:
            addresses, ttl = self.resolve(name)
            self._store(name, addresses, now + ttl)
            return addresses
        except LookupError as error:
            self._store(name, error, now + self.negative_ttl)
            raise

    def _store(self, name, value, expires):
        self.entries[name] = (value, expires)
        self.entries.move_to_end(name)
        if len(self.entries) > self.max_entries:
            self.entries.popitem(last=False)

Complexity: O(1) average per lookup and insert; O(max_entries) memory.

Design points: negative caching stops hammering the resolver for a missing name, but keep it short so a newly created record shows up fast; cap TTLs both ways (a min avoids hot loops, a max limits staleness); concurrent misses for the same name should share one in flight lookup (single flight) to avoid a stampede; serve stale on resolver failure is a useful resilience option.

Follow-ups: thread safety, prefetching popular names before expiry, why JVM style cache-forever breaks failover.

fields.Fact: A good DNS cache honours TTLs, caches failures briefly and coalesces concurrent misses.

fields.Question: Coding: without an HTTP library, write code that performs an HTTPS GET for a URL and returns the status code and body. What does the library normally handle for you?
fields.Answer:
import socket, ssl
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

def https_get(url, timeout=5.0):
    parts = urlsplit(url)
    host, port = parts.hostname, parts.port or 443
    path = (parts.path or "/") + (f"?{parts.query}" if parts.query else "")
    ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
    with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=timeout) as raw:
        with ctx.wrap_socket(raw, server_hostname=host) as tls:
            request = (f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {host}\r\n"
                       "Connection: close\r\nAccept-Encoding: identity\r\n\r\n")
            tls.sendall(request.encode("ascii"))
            chunks = []
            while data := tls.recv(65536):
                chunks.append(data)
    head, _, body = b"".join(chunks).partition(b"\r\n\r\n")
    status = int(head.split(b" ", 2)[1])
    return status, body

Why it works: create_connection does getaddrinfo and tries each address; wrap_socket with server_hostname sends SNI and verifies the certificate and hostname; Connection: close lets us read until EOF instead of parsing framing.

What libraries add: connection pooling and keep-alive, Content-Length and chunked parsing, redirects, decompression, proxies, HTTP/2, retries, cookies, timeouts per phase.

Pitfall: the body may be chunked even with Connection: close, so this simplified reader returns raw chunked data in that case.

Follow-ups: add chunked decoding, support keep-alive reuse, why you must never pass check_hostname=False.
